 How an El Niño winter could worsen pollution in Delhi
 Lower temperatures, wind speed and rain all contribute to an increased accumulation of pollutants in the air.
 Vaishnavi Rathore 
 18 hours ago

 Arun Sankar/AFP
 On October 21, the morning after Dusshera, Delhi-NCR woke up to a pollution haze, with the air quality index jumping to 244 – the worst in the last 100 days. This marked the beginning of the air pollution season, and the air is set to get worse through the winter as a result of continued vehicular emissions, construction and stubble burning.
 But this year, Delhi and the rest of the Indo-Gangetic plain faces an additional challenge that could worsen the air quality – an El Niño with “ unprecedented strength ”, expected to peak between November and January.
 El Niño is a climate pattern that repeats every few years. Influenced by warming sea surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific, it can increase heat and reduce rainfall across the world. Between the coming months of November and January, the sea surface temperature could rise 3.8 degree Celsius above average, making this year a “Super El Niño” year, the World Meteorological Organisation has predicted .
 While El Niño is not itself a source of pollution, meteorological factors associated with it, like temperature and wind speed, can affect the way pollutants mix in the atmosphere, and thus affect air quality.
 Gufran Beig, chair professor at the National Institute of Advanced Studies in Bengaluru, and founder-director of the System of Air Quality Forecasting and Research, explained that normal winter months already see a greater accumulation of pollutants in the air. This is because wind speeds are lower during this period, which can reduce the dispersal of pollutants – in contrast, in the summer and monsoon seasons, pollutants rise with hotter air, and faster winds disperse them.
 An El Niño scenario could “enhance the normal levels of weather trapping” by reducing wind speeds further, said Beig. Additionally, it could reduce the occurrence of western disturbances, a phenomenon that causes rain and snow in the Himalayas – this, in turn, can result in rain in north-western India, which helps flush out pollutants.
 Both these factors could cause pollutants to remain suspended in air for longer and “much more than what it normally does in this season”, Beig said.
 Local and global winds 
 Wind conditions in a particular region are determined by the interaction of local weather with global winds. The local conditions are temporary and specific to smaller regions, and are typically observed closer to the ground. For instance, Beig noted, coastal regions tend to see fast-moving local winds caused by the difference between ocean and land temperatures.
 Meanwhile, global “background winds” have a strong influence on overall wind behaviour, he added. These winds are influenced by temperature changes associated with phenomena such as El Niño, and its opposing, cooling phenomenon, La Nina.
 Delhi-NCR had an AQI of 244 on October 21, the morning after Dusshera. This was the worst air quality the region has seen in the last 100 days. Photo: Arun Sankar/AFP During an El Niño event, Pacific winds that usually move from South America to Asia weaken or slow down, and sometimes even reverse their direction back to South America. This impacts rainfall patterns – it brings very wet conditions to the west coast of South America, and leaves Asia unusually dry. This is why, with an active El Niño this year, India experienced a 13% monsoon deficit.
 This slowing of global winds can impact local meteorological conditions. Beig explained that “When large-scale wind circulation becomes slow because of a global phenomenon”, the already slower and weaker local winds of the winter months “will become even weaker”.
 These weaker winds are relatively ineffective at dispersing and flushing out pollutants, he added – this problem grows more serious over the months as El Niño peaks and air pollution intensifies.
 Previous El Niño years 
 Experts have noted a correlation between previous El Niño years and poor air quality.
 The Council on Energy, Environment and Water, or CEEW, examined air quality data between 2020 and 2024 – while 2023-’24 was an El Niño year, the other years were influenced by La Nina, the cooler global weather phenomenon, with faster winds.
 They found that between November and January, the number of “very poor” and “severe” AQI days were higher in the El Niño year of 2023-’24, compared to the La Nina years. For instance, December 2023 had 27 such days, compared to 25, 21 and 20 in the previous three years. The distinction was even more pronounced for January – the El Niño year had 30 “very poor” and “severe” days, while the other years had 20 or fewer such days.
 “Our study was based on just four years,” explained Prarthana Borah, a fellow at CEEW, who leads the air quality team. “And based on that, we can say that we did see the number of polluted days increase with El Niño year. This shows that there is a need to look deeper into these correlations.”
 Meanwhile, in a 2026 paper , Beig and others looked at PM2.5 concentrations in cities through the La Nina year of 2022-’23 and the El Niño year of 2023-’24.
 The study focused on two cities: Jaipur in the north and Hyderabad in the south. In Jaipur, they found that rainfall in the winter months of the La Nina year lowered PM2.5 concentrations, while the subsequent El Niño year saw less rainfall, which led to “less effective removal of atmospheric particles”.
 Research has also drawn links between El-Niño years and weaker western disturbances.
 A 2017 paper found that in 2015, El Niño conditions in the tropical Pacific Ocean led to increased sea-surface temperature of the northern parts of the Indian ocean, near peninsular India. This atypical change of temperature between the sea and peninsular India led to a “branching and weakening of westerly jet streams”, which in turn led to weaker winds over north-west India, fewer western disturbances and “meagre precipitation” in the region that winter.
 Experts noted that a poor monsoon in an El-Niño year can increase risks to air pollution in other ways also. Roxy Mathew Koll, climate scientist at Pune’s Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology, explained that a weak monsoon delays the sowing of kharif crops like paddy, thereby increasing the possibility of a delayed and reduced harvest. “When harvests are pushed back, the window before rabi sowing becomes even tighter,” Koll said. This increases pressure on farmers “to burn crop residue”, he noted.
 La Nina years 
 CEEW and Beig have also studied La Nina years closely. They found that in contrast to El Niño years, in these periods, higher wind speeds can lead to lower than average pollution, even in the winter.
 CEEW’s study found that in the La Nina winters between 2020 and 2023, the lower numbers of “very poor” and “severe” pollution days “can be attributed, at least in part, to higher wind speeds”.
 Similarly, in a 2024 paper , Beig and other scientists looked at air quality through the 2022-’23 La Nina year and found a “noticeable declining trend” of PM2.5 levels in most north Indian cities. For instance, compared to the “averaged winter values of the past three-years” Ghaziabad had a 33% reduction of PM2.5 levels, Rohtak a 30% reduction and Noida a 28% reduction.
 This study also found that this reduction was connected with faster winds. Usually, the study noted, winds that blow towards Delhi and surrounding areas dump stubble-induced pollutants to the Indo-Gangetic regions, including Delhi. But the winds in November 2022 were “relatively faster”, and carried pollutants away from the city.
 Tackling the problem 
 Experts argued that more long-term studies were needed, to make stronger correlations between air quality and climatic trends.
 “Meteorological conditions are complex, and isolating winds or temperatures to air pollution is difficult,” said Borah. While recent short-term studies do suggest “that meteorology plays a major role”, Borah said, “we do not have enough long-term and larger studies to exactly say what the impact is”.
 Experts also noted that even as studies make this connection between climate and air pollution clearer, it is imperative that pollution is curbed more effectively at sources.
 “During cold weather, whether we have El Niño or not, it will slow down wind speed and reduce the possibility of air pollutants’ dispersal,” said Borah. Further, she explained, apart from year-round vehicular pollution, the season also sees a rise in other sources of air pollution, like the burning of wood and other materials in the city, which people do to keep warm, and seasonal burning of agricultural residue. “All of these would need to be targeted,” Borah said.
 Borah explained that while Delhi has technologies like an early warning system developed by the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology, which gives up to 10-day forecasts of air quality, “We need to start using these and being more pro-active with these”, rather than reacting only when air quality deteriorates.
 Koll echoed the argument that pollution needed to be controlled at its sources. Farmers should get “timely, affordable help to manage crop residue, while cities must cut their own emissions from transport, industry, construction, and waste burning”, he said. He added, “We have enough warning to act before these pressures come together.”
 For Beig, too, the findings of the recent research studies are a reminder to move towards air pollution mitigation more urgently. “These relationships are showing us that we have to be even faster in curbing anthropogenic causes of air pollution,” he said.
